overview: Summerset Group Holdings is one of New Zealand's largest retirement village developers and operators, developing, building, and operating a portfolio of 44 villages across New Zealand with an expanding presence in Victoria, Australia. Founded in 1997 and listed on the NZX in 2011 (also ASX-listed as SNZ), the company operates under the Occupation Right Agreement (ORA) model whereby residents pay an upfront licence fee for the right to occupy a unit, with Summerset earning a Deferred Management Fee (DMF) of 25% of the ORA price when they leave. At FY2025 year-end, total assets stood at NZ$9.2 billion with 8,673 total units in portfolio, 9,500+ residents, and a land bank of 5,499 retirement units across both countries.

business_model.summary: Capital-intensive ORA model: residents pay upfront for occupation rights, generating DMF income on exit (typically 25% of ORA price over five years) plus recurring care fees and village services. Revenue is predominantly recurring from operations (~62% care fees/village services, ~37% DMF income), supplemented by one-off development margin on new unit sales. NTA growth is a key value driver as the portfolio appreciates.
business_model.customer_type: B2C - primarily retirees aged 70+ seeking independent living with continuum-of-care access
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~94% (637 of 693 units delivered in FY25), Australia ~6% (56 units delivered, 4 villages in Victoria). NZ portfolio spans 40 villages across 11 regions; Australia has 4 villages under development in metropolitan Melbourne and Geelong.

main_competitors: Ryman Healthcare (RYM.NZ) - largest NZ operator, ~50 villages, facing debt and capital raise challenges
Arvida Group (ARV.NZ) - third major NZ player, growth via acquisitions, recently taken private by Stonepeak
Metlifecare - private operator, ~35 villages, taken private by EQT in 2021
Oceania Healthcare (OCA.NZ) - listed NZX, care-heavy model
Bupa Care Services NZ - large private aged care operator
RetireAustralia - major Australian operator in SUM's target market
competitive_position.market_position: One of the 'big three' listed NZ retirement village operators. Summerset claims the largest and most diverse land bank in the NZ retirement village industry (5,499 units). Leads NZ market in overall brand 'consideration' and 'first choice' metrics. Care centre occupancy of 94% is above the industry average of ~90%.

moat_factors.description: Summerset holds the largest land bank in the NZ retirement village sector (5,499 retirement units plus 1,173 care units), providing a multi-decade development runway without needing to compete for expensive new sites. This pipeline took years and significant capital to assemble.

moat_factors.factor: Broadacre development model and in-house capability
moat_factors.description: Fully integrated in-house capability across land acquisition, planning, consenting, design, procurement and construction. This drives cost discipline and the ability to flex build rates with market conditions - a key competitive advantage vs. Ryman which outsources more. Development margins consistently 20-29%, well above the 20-25% medium-term target.

91% village and 89% care resident satisfaction. Seven consecutive years as Highly Commended Trusted Brand (Reader's Digest). Named Customer Champion by Australian Financial Review. These reinforce strong demand and support pricing power.

The ORA model creates inherent stickiness - residents make a significant capital commitment and face emotional and practical barriers to moving. DMF accrues at 5% per year (capped at 25% after 5 years), incentivising longer stays which benefit Summerset.

44 villages across 11 NZ regions plus 4 Australian sites provide resilience to local property market weakness. Only 43% of resales come from Auckland/Wellington/Christchurch, reducing concentration risk. Allows prudent management of build rates by region.

Ability for residents to move from independent living to care within the same village reduces churn risk. Care ORA conversion programme significantly improved Care EBITDA from $2.7m (FY24) to $18.8m (FY25). Target of $20-25k care EBITDA per bed medium-term.

weaknesses: High absolute debt ($1.97b interest-bearing debt) exposes balance sheet to interest rate rises and requires disciplined management
Care funding inadequacy: government funding increases lag wage cost inflation, limiting profitability of the care business
Limited to one country's property cycle in the medium term - if NZ property values decline materially, NTA and development margins compress
Early-stage Australia operations not yet profitable; execution risk on scaling to target 300 units/year by end of FY27
Ryman's reduced development pace may advantage Summerset short term but could allow Ryman to recover and compete more aggressively later

growth_drivers: Demographic tailwind: NZ population aged 75+ expected to double by 2048 and nearly triple over 50 years; Victoria, Australia over-75 population expected to increase from ~550,000 to ~1.2m over 40 years. This underpins sustained demand growth for decades.

Australia expansion: 4 villages in Victoria now under development (Cranbourne North, Chirnside Park, Oakleigh South, Torquay), plus planning permit for Mornington. Target of ~300 units/year Australia by end of FY27. First continuum-of-care offering launching in Australia in FY26.

Care ORA conversion programme: Converting standard care beds to ORA arrangements is significantly improving care profitability. Care EBITDA surged from $2.7m (FY24) to $18.8m (FY25) and company is targeting $20-25k average Care EBITDA per bed over the medium term.

Portfolio maturation and resale gains compounding: As portfolio grows and ages, resale volumes increase organically. Resale gains reached $104.5m in FY25 (up 9% YoY) with 10 villages generating 30+ resales. Average gross resale proceeds $582,000 per unit. This creates a growing recurring earnings stream that doesn't require capital deployment.

Land bank monetisation: 5,499-unit land bank provides growth runway to almost double portfolio size. In NZ, FY26 build guidance of 650-700 homes maintains steady delivery pace. Consenting programme progressing with resource consents received for Rotorua, Mosgiel and Belmont (Auckland).

Interest rate tailwinds: As RBNZ cuts interest rates, property market conditions improve, supporting higher ORA pricing, lower finance costs, and improved buyer confidence among retirees (who often need to sell existing homes to fund ORA).

Technology and operational efficiency: Lumin platform rolling out to all 39 villages in FY26, remote National Clinical Support nursing service expanding to all NZ care centres, AI tools for care staff, robotic lawnmowers and vacuum cleaners - all reducing cost per resident.

NZ construction procurement excellence: Won CIPS Australasia Best Procurement Transformation award. Sustained cost discipline and standardisation maintain development margins even in an inflationary environment.

business.risk: Property market downturn reducing resale activity and ORA pricing
business.description: Summerset's DMF income, development margin and NTA are all linked to residential property values. A prolonged NZ property downturn (as seen 2022-2024) reduces ORA prices, slows resale turnover, compresses development margins, and reduces investment property valuations. NZ property market was described as 'subdued' in FY25 - despite this, Summerset still delivered record sales, showing business resilience, but a sharper downturn could materially impact results.

business.risk: Uncontracted stock accumulation and slow sell-down
business.description: St Johns and Boulcott - two major metro Auckland and Wellington villages - have larger-than-usual apartment stock to sell through. As at FY25, 541 new units and 208 resale units were available for sale (9.7% of portfolio). Management is focused on sell-down ahead of further deliveries in FY26.

Government funding rates for care increase at a lower rate than actual wage and operational cost inflation, particularly for nursing staff. Care EBITDA per bed remains at only ~$13k in completed villages vs the $20-25k target. An Aged Care Advisory Group was formed in October 2025 and is expected to report to government in June 2026, but outcomes are uncertain.

Build cost inflation reduces development margins. While Summerset has partially offset through procurement improvements and standardisation (development margin 27.8% in FY25, above 20-25% medium-term guidance), sustained cost inflation could erode margins below target.

financial.description: Interest-bearing debt of $1,971m (21% of total assets) creates meaningful interest cost. Finance costs were $32m in FY25 vs $26m in FY24 (+22%). The company uses interest rate swaps to partially hedge. Gearing ratio of 37.1% is within the 30-40% target band but leaves limited headroom. Debt expected to keep rising as Australian investment increases before reaching scale.

financial.risk: Capital intensity and ongoing funding requirement
financial.description: CapEx was $722m in FY25 (vs operating cash flow of $548m), with the difference funded by debt. Core debt is zero (operating villages self-fund), but development debt continues to accumulate during construction phases. The business has no core debt per management, but total debt will continue to rise before Australia generates meaningful cash flow.

Growing Australian operations create NZD/AUD translation exposure. A weaker AUD reduces the NZD value of Australian assets and any eventual earnings. In FY25, $8.5m loss on translation of foreign currency operations was recorded in other comprehensive income.

regulatory.description: NZ Government announced December 2025 plans to amend the Retirement Villages Act in 2026, including: ceasing weekly fees after a resident vacates, preventing charging for chattels maintenance, paying interest after 6 months if a home is unsold, and mandatory 12-month buy-back if homes remain unsold. Summerset says its practices already largely align with proposed changes. However, the 12-month mandatory buy-back (if enacted) could create liquidity pressure in a weak market, and concerns remain about impact on smaller operators and the broader system. Bill expected to go to Parliament during 2026.

Australia's new Aged Care Act came into force November 2025. Summerset's Australian operations team has worked throughout FY25 to meet requirements. First aged care operations in Australia expected to commence FY26 at Cranbourne North - any compliance failures could delay the rollout and damage brand.

regulatory.risk: Care sector funding model reform risk
regulatory.description: Any changes to New Zealand's aged care funding model could have material positive or negative impacts. Current inadequacy limits care profitability; a positive reform could significantly boost earnings. Adverse reform or continued underfunding constrains the care business.

macro.risk: Interest rates and NZ economic slowdown
macro.description: NZ economic environment remained challenging through 2025, though signs of optimism are emerging. Higher interest rates slow property market activity, reduce the appetite of retirees to sell existing homes to move into villages, and increase Summerset's own finance costs. The RBNZ began cutting the OCR in 2024 and is expected to continue, which is a tailwind.

Operating expenses grew 16% in FY25 ($328.6m vs $284.1m), driven by staff costs (58% of opex), inflationary pressures, and start-up costs. NZ construction and healthcare labour markets remain tight, with wages increasing faster than care funding subsidies.

NZ house prices have been subdued since peaking in late 2021. Improving conditions as of late 2025, but any re-deterioration would reduce ORA pricing power, slow sales, and pressure fair value movements. The 2025 investment property fair value gain of $264.5m assumes improving property market trajectory.

execution.description: Summerset is in the early stages of Australian expansion with only 88 units delivered at Cranbourne North and 10 at Chirnside Park by FY25 year-end. Scaling to ~300 units per year by end of FY27 requires hiring, training, supply chain development, accreditation, and operational setup across 4+ simultaneous sites in an unfamiliar regulatory and market environment. Any delays, cost overruns, or demand shortfalls in Australia could significantly impact both capital allocation and financial results.

New CFO Margaret Warrington joined February 2025. Chief Sales Officer Fay French stepped back from ELT due to health; Chief Marketing Officer Kay Brodie planning to retire during 2026. These roles are being consolidated into a new Chief Sales and Marketing Officer role, with David Martin joining January 2026. Changes at senior level during an expansion phase carry some transition risk.

FY25 saw the highest ever number of simultaneous commercial builds (12 projects active in NZ). Five more village centre buildings are due in the next 12 months. Village centres contain care centres, serviced apartments and amenities - they are more complex and carry lower development margins than villas. Delivery delays or cost overruns would impact near-term results.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ retirement village sector has strong demographic tailwinds: the over-75 population is set to double by 2048. JLL estimates demand for retirement units increasing by ~2,200/year, creating a growing supply-demand gap. Industry residency rate expected to increase from ~45,000 to ~68,000 by 2028. Industry is structurally sound but near-term trading conditions have been impacted by NZ property market weakness and a constrained economic environment. The sector is showing early signs of recovery as interest rates fall. In Australia, Victoria's over-75 population expected to more than double over 40 years, and the retirement village penetration rate is lower than NZ, presenting a large opportunity.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high cyclicality tied to residential property market. Business fundamentals (DMF, care fees) are relatively stable, but development margins, NTA growth, and new sales velocity are all correlated with property prices and buyer confidence. Resale activity is also linked to general property market liquidity. However, demographic demand provides a structural floor that limits downside.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - dual sensitivity: (1) Rising rates increase finance costs on $1.97b debt directly; (2) Higher rates reduce NZ property market activity, slowing ORA sales as retirees struggle to sell existing homes. RBNZ rate cuts in 2024-2025 are a meaningful tailwind. Management expects gearing to decline as the portfolio matures.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Limited but growing AUD/NZD exposure as Australian operations scale. All reporting is in NZD.
key_input_costs: Construction materials (concrete, steel, timber) - standardised designs and procurement programmes partially mitigate
Healthcare labour (nurses, caregivers) - largest operating cost at 58% of opex, exposed to minimum wage and sector wage inflation
Insurance and council rates - both increasing above CPI
Energy costs - accelerating transition to solar and away from gas to reduce exposure

recent_developments.event: FY2025 full year results released (27 Feb 2026): Record underlying profit $234.2m (+13%), record 1,560 ORA sales (+26%), 693 units delivered, NTA $13.75/share (+$1.32 YoY), total assets $9.2b. IFRS net profit $259.7m (down 22% on FY24 due to lower fair value movements). Final dividend 13.2 cps declared, payable 26 March 2026 (full year 24.5 cps, flat vs FY24).

NZ Government announced December 2025 plans to amend Retirement Villages Act in 2026, including mandatory 12-month buy-back and cessation of weekly fees post-vacate. Bill expected to go to Parliament during 2026. Summerset says its practices already largely align. Care house prices regulation proposal also announced.

First villas delivered at Chirnside Park (second Australian village), with 60% of the first 28 homes released pre-sold. Village centre building at Cranbourne North completed - Australia's first continuum-of-care facility for Summerset. Construction commenced at Oakleigh South (fourth Australian village).

Australian new Aged Care Act came into force on 1 November 2025. Summerset has been working throughout FY25 to ensure compliance and expects to begin providing aged care at Cranbourne North in Q2 FY26.

Sod-turning event at Summerset Oakleigh South (fourth Australian village). Named a Customer Champion by the Australian Financial Review. Aged Care Advisory Group formed by NZ government to advise on sustainable care funding model.

Record H1 2025 results announced: underlying profit $106.6m (+19%), IFRS net profit $127.2m (+26%), 692 ORA sales (record first half, +18% on H1 2024), operating cash flow $228.7m (+19%). First residents moved into Summerset Rangiora (fifth Canterbury village).
Summerset St Johns received Excellence award at NZ Property Council Awards in the Retirement Living and Aged Care category.
Margaret Warrington joined as new Chief Financial Officer. Care centre at Summerset Boulcott opened.

David Martin joined as Chief Sales and Marketing Transformation Lead, consolidating previously separate sales and marketing functions. Partnership with Golf New Zealand commenced (naming rights of Charles Tour).

items.metric: NZ build rate (new homes delivered under ORA)
items.notes: Flat vs FY25 NZ delivery of 637 homes. Management keeping build rate stable to manage stock levels and focus on selling existing inventory, particularly at St Johns and Boulcott. Five village centre buildings scheduled for delivery in FY26.

items.metric: Australia build rate (new homes delivered under ORA)
items.notes: Increased from FY25 Australia delivery of 56 homes. Includes further deliveries at Cranbourne North and Chirnside Park (30-40 homes), plus early deliveries from Oakleigh South and Torquay targeted for FY27.

items.metric: Total build rate (combined NZ and Australia)
items.notes: Implied from NZ 650-700 and Australia 100-150 guidance ranges. Up from 693 total in FY25.
Strategic target reiterated. Requires scaling across Cranbourne North, Chirnside Park, Oakleigh South, Torquay and potentially Mornington by end of FY27.

FY25 achieved 27.8% (above guidance range) due to strong villa mix. Expected to track more within 20-25% range as more care centres and apartment suites settle in FY26, which carry lower development margins.
Currently at ~$13k per bed. Care ORA conversion programme and new care centres expected to drive this metric higher. FY25 total Care EBITDA was $18.8m, up from $2.7m in FY24.

FY25 year-end gearing of 37.1%, within target band. Management expects aggregate net debt growth to reduce in FY26 as village centre building delivery pipeline completes and sell-through occurs. Total debt $1.97b vs target band of $2.0-2.5b.
Board adopted a formal three-year review cycle for dividend policy. Policy will be reviewed during FY26. FY25 distribution was 25.3% of underlying profit (24.5 cps full year, flat on FY24).

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Scott Scoullar: 'We continue to believe in our value proposition in both New Zealand and Australia going into FY26. Even in constrained trading conditions we have continued to see extremely high demand and record sales numbers.' Management is focused on three key areas signalled at H1 2025: operating cost management, Australian progress, and debt tracking. Operating expense growth was $10.2m in 2H25, down from $14m in 1H25, demonstrating the cost discipline programme is working. Management expressed optimism about improving NZ property market conditions as they move into 2026, with external valuers lifting unit pricing and growth rate assumptions. No earnings guidance was provided for FY2026.

bull_case: Demographic tailwind is the most powerful structural growth driver in the NZ and Australian investment universe. NZ's 75+ population doubling by 2048, creating decades of compound demand growth for Summerset's 5,499-unit land bank pipeline at virtually no marginal land acquisition cost.

Australia expansion is now gaining real momentum: Cranbourne North village centre delivered, Chirnside Park villas 60% pre-sold immediately, four villages under construction simultaneously. If Summerset replicates its NZ model in Australia, this doubles its total addressable market. Early evidence (Customer Champion award, strong presales) suggests brand is resonating.

Resale gains are a compounding, capital-light income stream. With 32 villages generating resales and 10 villages achieving 30+ resales in FY25, as the portfolio matures the resale flywheel spins faster. Average resale proceeds of $582,000 and embedded value of $1.9b represents future cash that requires no additional capital deployment.

Interest rate cuts in NZ (RBNZ OCR was cut significantly from its 2024 peak) reduce finance costs, improve NZ property market conditions (helping both ORA pricing and retiree ability to sell existing homes), and expand NTA valuations. Summerset is operationally leveraged to a normalising interest rate environment.

Summerset's balance sheet and operational discipline sharply differentiates it from Ryman Healthcare (which has required two large capital raises totalling ~$2b since 2023 and has largely paused development). Summerset's model - broadacre, in-house construction, disciplined land procurement - has preserved margins at 27.8% through a difficult cycle and maintained gearing within its target band.
bear_case: Interest-bearing debt of $1.97b (approaching the $2.0b lower end of management's $2-2.5b target band) leaves limited balance sheet headroom. Any unexpected stress - prolonged NZ property downturn, major construction cost blowout, or Australian ramp-up delays - could require dilutive equity issuance or force a painful build rate reduction.

Australian execution risk is significant and often underestimated. Building retirement villages in an unfamiliar regulatory, labour, and construction market from a standing start is complex. Cranbourne North and Chirnside Park are very early stage; reaching 300 units/year by end of FY27 from just 56 units in FY25 is an ambitious target. Any delays, cost overruns, or demand shortfalls could impair returns and require further capital.

NZ Retirement Villages Act reform, while Summerset says its practices already align, introduces the mandatory 12-month buy-back obligation. This creates potential liquidity risk in a weak market and could impact the financial model for smaller operators - if the broader sector is stressed, it creates systemic reputational and demand risk.

Care business structural headwinds: Government aged care funding consistently lags wage cost inflation, particularly for nursing staff. With 58% of operating costs being employee expenses, sustained above-CPI wage growth in a sector with chronic labour shortages creates a persistent earnings drag on the care operations that the Care ORA conversion programme only partially offsets.

NTA-per-share of $13.75 provides some valuation support, but IFRS net profit is highly volatile (swinging from $332m in FY24 to $259m in FY25) due to fair value movements. If the NZ property recovery stalls or reverses, fair value gains could turn to losses, and the IFRS earnings narrative becomes negative even if underlying profit continues growing - confusing investors and potentially pressuring the stock.
